title: Arguments, quoted arrays and option boundaries
markdown:
## Why this matters

A script receives its arguments as separate values, and the first thing many scripts do is destroy that separation: joining them into one string, splitting them again, and then passing a filename with a space to a command as two names. The same script is then handed a file called `-report.csv` and the command treats it as an option. Both failures come from one idea: argument boundaries are data, and the script must forward them unchanged.

## The simple version

Think of arguments as a stack of index cards. `"$@"` hands the cards over one by one, untouched. `"$*"` glues them into one card with spaces between, and `$@` without quotes shuffles the cards through the shell's word splitting again, so a card that contained a space becomes two. An array such as `files=("$@")` keeps a copy of the stack that you can grow, shorten or forward later.

The analogy breaks at option parsing: even a perfectly forwarded card that begins with `-` is read by the receiving command as an instruction rather than a name. That is a second boundary, and the receiving command decides it, not the shell.

## Core mechanics

`$1`, `$2` and `$#` address positional parameters; `shift` drops the first one. `"$@"` expands to each argument as its own word and is the only correct way to forward all of them. `for arg in "$@"` (or simply `for arg`) iterates without splitting. Storing arguments in an array, `args=("$@")`, and expanding `"${args[@]}"` preserves the same boundaries.

Most GNU commands accept `--` to mark the end of options, after which every argument is an operand even if it starts with a hyphen: `wc -l -- "$@"`. When a command lacks `--`, prefix the name with `./` to make it a path. `set -- "$@" extra` appends to the positional parameters without losing existing boundaries.

## Failure modes

`for f in $*` splits every argument on whitespace and expands globs inside them. Building a command as a string, `cmd="wc -l $file"` then `$cmd`, re-splits the filename and cannot represent an argument containing a space at all. Checking `[ -z $1 ]` without quotes turns an empty first argument into a syntax error; use `[ -z "$1" ]` or `[[ -z $1 ]]`. Treating `$#` as a string comparison instead of a number hides the "no arguments" case.

## Runnable experiment

Save this as `argv.sh`, make it executable, and predict each result before running.

```bash
#!/bin/bash
printf 'argc=%s\n' "$#"
for arg; do printf '<%s>\n' "$arg"; done
printf 'joined=%s\n' "$*"
args=("$@")
printf 'array=%s\n' "${#args[@]}"
wc -l -- "$@" 2>&1 | sed 's/^/wc: /'
```

```bash
touch 'quarterly report.txt' -- '-report.csv'
./argv.sh 'quarterly report.txt' -report.csv ''
# argc=3, three bracketed values (the last empty), joined as one string,
# array=3, and wc counts both files because -- ends option parsing.
./argv.sh $(printf 'quarterly report.txt')
# argc=2: unquoted command substitution split the name.
```

## Practical exercise

Write `safe_count`, a wrapper that forwards every argument to `wc -l` without splitting or option confusion, refuses to run with zero arguments (usage message to stderr, exit status 2), and prints each result with the exact filename. Test it with a plain name, a name with spaces, a name starting with a hyphen, an empty argument and no arguments. Record the transcript and mark which behaviors come from the shell and which from `wc`.

Test a plain name, a spaced name, a leading-hyphen name, an empty argument and no arguments.

hints: "$@" keeps each argument as one word; "$*" joins them.
Check the argument count with [ "$#" -eq 0 ], not by testing $1 for emptiness.
Quote every expansion inside [ ]; an empty unquoted value is a syntax error.

questions.prompt: Which expansion forwards all script arguments to `wc -l` with their original boundaries?
questions.explanation: "$@" expands to each argument as a separate word; the other forms join or re-split.

questions.prompt: A file is named `-report.csv`. Which invocation counts its lines?
questions.explanation: Quoting only affects the shell; -- tells wc that what follows is an operand.

questions.prompt: `args=("$@")` followed by `for f in "${args[@]}"` differs from `for f in $*` because…
choices: the quoted array iteration keeps each argument intact while $* re-splits on whitespace
questions.correct_answer: the quoted array iteration keeps each argument intact while $* re-splits on whitespace
questions.explanation: Quoted array expansion preserves boundaries; unquoted $* undergoes word splitting and globbing.
questions.learning_objective: Store and iterate arguments with an array

questions.prompt: Why does `[ -z $1 ]` fail when the script is called with an empty first argument?
questions.correct_answer: The empty value vanishes, leaving [ -z ] which is a syntax error. Unquoted empty expansions disappear; quote them inside test.
questions.explanation: Unquoted empty expansions disappear; quote them inside test.

questions.prompt: Explain the two separate boundaries involved when a script forwards the filename `-quarterly report.csv` to a command.
questions.correct_answer: The shell boundary: the name must be forwarded as one argument, which "$@" or a quoted array does. The option boundary: the receiving command reads a leading hyphen as an option, so the script must pass -- before operands or use a ./ path form. Quoting fixes only the first.
questions.explanation: Shell argument construction and program option parsing are independent boundaries.
questions.learning_objective: Separate shell boundaries from option parsing
